question: What is the meaning of building identification in relation to product context?
description: Building identification in relation to product context refers to the process of uniquely identifying and tracking products and materials within a building throughout their entire lifecycle. This is crucial for managing the materials and products in a building, especially when decommissioning or taking apart the building. The unique identifiers help in tracing the whereabouts of materials and products, ensuring that their information can still be reconstructed. This process is essential for a materials passport system, which aims to promote a circular economy by enabling the reuse and recycling of materials. The unique identifiers also facilitate the tracking of products and materials for transportation and logistics purposes.

4.3.3.1.1. Product. Product is central to the use case of this study. 
According to ISO/DIS 59004, product is defined as “physical-based object 
designed for or utilized with a purpose”. Examples of products include 
goods of any type, hardware. and processed materials. This definition is 
adopted to annotate the Product key notion in our ontology. 
In the context of aligning with existing ontologies, we examined 
similar classes from various ontologies: BOT's Element, defined as ‘a 
construction entity with a characteristic technical function, form, or position’; 
BPO's Product, described as ‘a description of any item that can be or is 
offered for sale by vendors or manufacturers’; Brick's Equipment, which 
includes ‘devices that serve all or part of the building and may include electric 
power, lighting, transportation, or service water heating, including, but not 
limited to, furnaces, boilers, air conditioners, heat pumps, chillers, water 
heaters, lamps, luminaires, ballasts, elevators, escalators, or other devices or 
installations’; and REC's Asset, characterized as ‘something which is placed 
inside of a building, but is not an integral part of that building's structure; e.g., 
furniture, equipment, systems, etc.’ Our Product class, adopting a broader 
definition from ISO/DIS 59004, encapsulates these specific entities, 
positioning them as specialized instances within our broader Product 
framework. This enables shared definitions of concepts and promotes 
semantic interoperability and standardization of the key notion. Table 6 
presents the Product module alignment with the existing ontologies in 
the built environment space. 
Following the identified information requirements, products should 
be represented by names and unique identifiers, for which the Name Stub 
and Identifier ontology design patterns are selected; see Fig. 3.
